aspects.says: A bound reference evaluates the expression before :: once, when the reference is created, while a lambda evaluates it on every call.
basis: section:A Bound Receiver Is Evaluated Once, When the Reference Is Created

aspects.says: javac hands most method references to LambdaMetafactory as a direct handle to the named method, with no lambda$ method; varargs, array constructors and super:: get an adapter.
basis: section:javac Points Most Method References Straight at the Method, With No lambda$ Method in Between

aspects.says: A lambda reads better than a method reference when the call swaps arguments, adds a constant or chains calls.
basis: section:A Lambda Reads Better When the Call Needs Swapped Arguments, a Constant, or a Chain
aspects.reason: a judgement of readability: both forms behave the same, so no test can tell a reader's choice apart

aspects.says: A bound reference with a null receiver throws a NullPointerException without a message where it is created; the lambda throws only when called.
basis: section:A Null Receiver Fails Where the Reference Is Created

aspects.says: A method reference compiles when its call fits the target interface's method; javac does not check that the method means what the interface's contract asks for.
basis: section:A Method Reference Is a Lambda That Makes One Call, and the Target Type Decides What the Call Means

aspects.says: A stack trace through a method reference has no frame for the reference itself; a JDK method failing on a null element leaves no frame of the caller's code and no NPE message.
basis: section:A Stack Trace Through a Method Reference Has No Frame of Its Own
